- **Elbow stiffness (post-traumatic):** functional arc **30-130 degrees (Morrey)** (**modern tasks need about 27-149 degrees**); **arthroscopic or open (column procedure) release**; **ulnar nerve decompression if flexion under about 90-100 degrees pre-op** (risk of post-op ulnar neuritis when flexion improves).

> Exam pearl: **Valgus torque in late cocking/early acceleration exceeds the UCL: flexor-pronator, radiocapitellar joint and olecranon share load. VEO = medial tension (UCL), lateral compression (capitellar OCD/Panner), posterior shear (posteromedial osteophytes).**

> Exam pearl: **UCL anterior bundle = primary valgus restraint 20-120 degrees; moving valgus stress test most sensitive (pain 70-120 degrees); MR arthrography T sign. Reconstruction (palmaris longus, docking), ulnar neuritis = commonest complication. Internal-brace repair for avulsions in young throwers.**

> Exam pearl: **Panner (under 10, whole capitellum, self-limiting) vs capitellar OCD (adolescents, focal, may need surgery: OATS for large/lateral-margin lesions). Medial epicondyle fracture: incarcerated fragment = absolute surgery; throwers fix over 2 mm. Distal biceps: hook test; single-incision = LABCN injury; two-incision = synostosis.**

hip arthroscopy and FAI.md:
## 1. Femoroacetabular impingement (FAI): concept
- **Abnormal contact between the proximal femur and acetabular rim** during motion (especially **flexion + internal rotation**): **labral tears and chondral damage**: a **cause of early OA** in young adults (Ganz).
- **Warwick Agreement (2016) definition of FAI syndrome:** **triad of symptoms (motion- or position-related hip/groin pain), clinical signs (positive impingement test, restricted internal rotation) and imaging findings (cam or pincer morphology)**. **Morphology alone is not FAI** (common in asymptomatic athletes).

## 2. Types
| | **Cam** | **Pincer** |
|---|---|---|
| Pathology | **Femoral**: **aspherical femoral head-neck junction** (reduced offset, "pistol-grip" deformity); jammed into the acetabulum in flexion/IR | **Acetabular**: **global or focal over-coverage** (retroversion, coxa profunda, protrusio) |
| Typical patient | **Young, athletic males** (adolescent sports during physeal closure: **repetitive loading of the developing physis**); **SCFE sequelae**, Perthes | **Middle-aged active women** |
| Damage pattern | **"Outside-in" abrasion**: **chondrolabral separation**, **delamination of the anterosuperior acetabular cartilage** (**carpet lesion/wave sign**): **more cartilage damage** | **Labral crushing/degeneration first** (linear contact); **contrecoup lesion posteroinferiorly** (head levered out); ossification of the labrum |
| Measures | **Alpha angle (over 55 degrees)** (Notzli; on 45-degree Dunn view or radial MRI), **head-neck offset ratio (under 0.17)**, **pistol-grip deformity**, **anterior offset** | **Crossover sign** (retroversion: anterior wall crosses the posterior wall), **posterior wall sign** (posterior wall medial to the head centre), **ischial spine sign** (projection of the ischial spine into the pelvis: retroversion), **lateral centre-edge angle (LCEA) over 40 degrees**, **coxa profunda (acetabular fossa medial to the ilioischial line)**, **protrusio (femoral head medial to ilioischial line)**, **Tönnis angle (acetabular index) under 0 degrees** |
- **Mixed (combined) FAI: commonest (about 70-85%)**.
- **Subspine (AIIS) impingement:** prominent **anterior inferior iliac spine** (Hetsroni types I-III) (**healed rectus femoris avulsion**): **AIIS decompression**.
- **Ischiofemoral impingement:** narrowing between the ischium and lesser trochanter (**quadratus femoris oedema** on MRI).
- **Femoral version abnormalities:** **femoral retroversion** worsens impingement; **excessive femoral anteversion/acetabular dysplasia**: **instability, not impingement**: hip arthroscopy alone may worsen symptoms.

## 3. Clinical evaluation
- **Groin pain ("C sign": hand cupped over the lateral hip)**, worse with **sitting, flexion, pivoting**, mechanical symptoms (catching, clicking), **reduced internal rotation in flexion**.
- **Tests:**
  - **FADIR (anterior impingement test: flexion, adduction, internal rotation)**: **highly sensitive, low specificity**,
  - **FABER (Patrick)**: posterior/SI or posterior impingement,
  - **Posterior impingement test** (extension + external rotation),
  - **Log roll** (instability/intra-articular),
  - **Dial test** (capsular laxity),
  - **Stinchfield (resisted straight leg raise)**: intra-articular pathology.
- **Diagnostic intra-articular local anaesthetic injection**: pain relief confirms an intra-articular source.

## 4. Imaging
- **AP pelvis (standardised: coccyx tip about 1-3 cm above the symphysis, centred)**: **crossover sign, posterior wall sign, ischial spine sign, LCEA, Tönnis angle, joint space (Tönnis OA grade)**, **pistol-grip deformity**.
- **45-degree Dunn view / frog-leg lateral / cross-table lateral**: **alpha angle, head-neck offset**.
- **False profile view (Lequesne)**: **anterior centre-edge angle (ACEA under 20 degrees = anterior undercoverage)**, AIIS.
- **MR arthrography (gadolinium) or 3T MRI** (labral tears: **anterosuperior** commonest, cartilage damage), **CT with 3D reconstruction** (cam/pincer mapping, **femoral version**, AIIS).

### Acetabular dysplasia and instability measures (important to exclude)
- **LCEA (Wiberg): normal 25-40 degrees**; **under 20 degrees = dysplasia**; **20-25 degrees = borderline dysplasia**.
- **Tönnis (acetabular) angle: normal 0-10 degrees**; **over 10 degrees = dysplasia (steep roof)**; **under 0 degrees = over-coverage (pincer)**.
- **Femoral head extrusion index** (over 25% = uncovered), **Shenton line break**, **FEAR index** (femoro-epiphyseal acetabular roof index: helps decide instability in borderline dysplasia).
- **Dysplasia (LCEA under 20) treatment = periacetabular osteotomy (PAO; Bernese/Ganz)**: **isolated arthroscopic labral debridement/capsulotomy in dysplasia can cause catastrophic instability**.

## 5. Indications and contraindications for FAI surgery
- **Indications:** **symptomatic FAI syndrome** failing non-operative management (**activity modification, physiotherapy (core and hip strengthening), NSAIDs, injection**) for at least about 3 months, with **preserved joint space**.
- **Contraindications / poor prognostic factors:** **established OA (Tönnis grade 2 or more, joint space under 2 mm)**: **poor outcomes; conversion to THA**, **older age (over 40-50)**, **significant dysplasia (LCEA under 20)** (unless combined with PAO), **severe chondral damage (Outerbridge IV)**, **high BMI**, workers' compensation.
- **Evidence:** **UK FASHIoN trial** (and **Australian FAIT**): **hip arthroscopy improved patient-reported outcomes more than best conservative care (physiotherapy)** at 12 months in FAI syndrome.

## 6. Surgical technique
- **Supine or lateral position on a traction table**, **well-padded perineal post** (or **post-less**), **traction (about 8-10 mm of joint distraction)**; **limit traction time to under about 2 hours** (**pudendal nerve neurapraxia** (perineal post), **sciatic nerve**, **lateral femoral cutaneous nerve** (anterior portal), **perineal skin injury**, **scrotal/labial injury**).
- **Portals:**
  - **Anterolateral (first; under fluoroscopy; 1 cm anterior and 1 cm superior to the greater trochanter tip)**: **superior gluteal nerve** (about 4-6 cm superior),
  - **Mid-anterior / anterior**: **lateral femoral cutaneous nerve (closest structure: about 3 mm)**, **femoral neurovascular bundle** (medial: avoid crossing the line from the ASIS downward),
  - **Posterolateral**: **sciatic nerve** (keep the leg in neutral/internal rotation).
- **Central compartment** (with traction): labrum, chondral surfaces, ligamentum teres, acetabular fossa; **peripheral compartment** (without traction, hip flexed): **head-neck junction (cam)**, synovium, loose bodies.
- **Interportal or T-capsulotomy**; **capsular repair/closure** (**reduces post-op instability**, especially in **borderline dysplasia, hyperlaxity, women**).
- **Pincer: acetabular rim trimming (acetabuloplasty)** with **labral takedown and re-fixation** (**avoid over-resection: iatrogenic instability/dysplasia**; LCEA should remain over 25 degrees).
- **Labrum: repair/refixation (suture anchors) preferred over debridement** (better outcomes; **labral seal effect**: maintains intra-articular fluid pressure, cartilage nutrition, stability); **labral reconstruction (allograft/ITB autograft)** for irreparable/deficient labra in young patients.
- **Cam: femoroplasty (osteochondroplasty)** of the head-neck junction under fluoroscopy and dynamic assessment; **avoid over-resection (over about 30% of the neck diameter: femoral neck fracture risk)**; **protect the retinacular (lateral epiphyseal) vessels** (**posterosuperior neck: branches of the medial femoral circumflex artery**: **avoid resection at the 12 o'clock-posterior region**: **AVN**).
- **Chondral lesions**: **microfracture** for small full-thickness acetabular lesions.
- **Open surgical hip dislocation (Ganz: trochanteric flip osteotomy, preserving the MFCA by staying anterior to the short external rotators; the obturator externus protects the deep branch)**: for **complex/global deformities (severe pincer, protrusio, posterior cam, Perthes deformity, SCFE)**.
- **Periacetabular osteotomy (PAO)** for dysplasia (± arthroscopy); **femoral derotation osteotomy** for abnormal version.

## 7. Complications of hip arthroscopy
- **Neurapraxia** (**pudendal (perineal post: commonest neurological), sciatic, femoral, LFCN**), **traction injuries**, **iatrogenic chondral/labral damage** (scuffing on portal entry), **instrument breakage**.
- **Heterotopic ossification** (**NSAID prophylaxis (naproxen) after femoroplasty**).
- **Iatrogenic instability/dislocation** (unrepaired capsulotomy, over-resection, dysplasia, hyperlaxity).
- **Femoral neck fracture** (over-resection), **AVN** (rare).
- **Abdominal fluid extravasation** (**intra-abdominal compartment syndrome**; risk with iliopsoas release, high pump pressure, prolonged surgery).
- **DVT**, **infection** (rare), **under-resection** (**residual impingement: commonest cause of revision**), **adhesions**.

## 8. Other hip arthroscopy indications and extra-articular conditions
- **Ligamentum teres tears** (instability, dysplasia), **loose bodies** (synovial chondromatosis, trauma), **septic arthritis** (washout), **pigmented villonodular synovitis (diffuse TGCT)**, **gluteus medius/minimus tears ("rotator cuff of the hip")**: **endoscopic or open repair**; **greater trochanteric pain syndrome** (gluteal tendinopathy: **education + loading exercise (LEAP trial) best long-term**; ESWT; steroid injection short-term).
- **Snapping hip:**
  - **External (ITB over the greater trochanter)**: **visible snap**; ITB release/Z-plasty,
  - **Internal (iliopsoas tendon over the iliopectineal eminence or femoral head)**: **audible snap**, **extension from a flexed-abducted-externally rotated position**; **iliopsoas release (at the lesser trochanter or transcapsular)** if refractory (weakness of hip flexion),
  - **Intra-articular** (labral tears, loose bodies).
- **Deep gluteal syndrome** (sciatic nerve entrapment: **piriformis**, fibrous bands): endoscopic decompression.
- **Athletic pubalgia ("sports hernia"/core muscle injury)** and **adductor-related groin pain** (**Doha agreement** classification: adductor-, iliopsoas-, inguinal-, pubic-related groin pain); **osteitis pubis**.
- **Femoral neck stress fractures:** **compression side (inferomedial: protected weight bearing; fix if fracture line over 50% of the neck width)** vs **tension side (superolateral: urgent internal fixation)** (**female athlete triad/RED-S**).

> Exam pearl: **Cam (young men, alpha angle over 55, outside-in chondral delamination) vs pincer (middle-aged women, crossover/posterior wall/ischial spine signs, LCEA over 40, contrecoup). Mixed commonest. FADIR sensitive.**

> Exam pearl: **Arthroscopy contraindicated with joint space under 2 mm/Tönnis 2+ and in dysplasia (LCEA under 20: needs PAO). Repair the labrum (seal) and the capsule. Avoid over-resection (neck fracture) and posterosuperior retinacular vessels (AVN). Under-resection = commonest cause of revision. FASHIoN: arthroscopy beats physio.**

> Exam pearl: **Portals: anterior portal = LFCN closest; anterolateral = superior gluteal nerve; posterolateral = sciatic nerve. Perineal post = pudendal neurapraxia. HO prophylaxis with NSAIDs. Fluid extravasation into the abdomen = abdominal compartment syndrome.**

## 1. Muscle injury and healing
- **Muscle strain:** commonest at the **myotendinous junction**, in **two-joint muscles** with **eccentric contraction** (**hamstrings (biceps femoris long head commonest)**, rectus femoris, medial gastrocnemius ("tennis leg"), adductor longus).
- **Healing phases:** **destruction/inflammation (days 1-3)**, **repair (regeneration of myofibres from satellite cells + scar formation, days 3-21)**, **remodelling** (weeks-months). **Satellite cells** = muscle stem cells.
- **Grading:** **grade I** (stretch, under 5% fibres), **II** (partial tear), **III** (complete rupture); **British Athletics Muscle Injury Classification (BAMIC)**: **0-4** with **a (myofascial), b (musculotendinous junction), c (intratendinous: longer return to play, higher recurrence)**.
- **Hamstring injuries:**
  - **Proximal hamstring avulsion** (**forced hip flexion with knee extension: water skiing**): **surgical repair** for **complete avulsion of 3 tendons**, or **2 tendons with over 2 cm retraction** in active patients; **early repair (within about 4-6 weeks)** gives better outcomes; **sciatic nerve** proximity.
  - **Prevention: Nordic hamstring eccentric programme** (reduces injuries by about 50%).
- **Treatment of muscle strains:** **PEACE & LOVE** (protection, elevation, avoid anti-inflammatories early, compression, education; load, optimism, vascularisation, exercise) has largely replaced **RICE/PRICE**; early controlled mobilisation; avoid immobilisation over a few days.
- **Delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS):** **24-72 hours after unaccustomed eccentric exercise**; microtrauma; **raised CK**; self-limiting.
- **Myositis ossificans** (after contusion, **quadriceps**): **zonal pattern (mature peripheral ossification, immature centre)** (vs osteosarcoma: **reverse zoning**); **avoid massage/aggressive stretching early**; excise only after maturation (**about 6-12 months, bone scan cold**) if symptomatic.
- **Exertional rhabdomyolysis:** **CK over 5 times normal (often over 10,000)**, **myoglobinuria (dark urine)**, **acute kidney injury**; **sickle cell trait**, heat, dehydration; **aggressive IV fluids**.

## 2. Tendon injury and tendinopathy
- **Tendon structure:** **type I collagen (about 95%)**, **tenocytes**, proteoglycans (**decorin**); hierarchy: fibril, fibre, fascicle, tendon; **endotenon/epitenon/paratenon (vascular, in tendons without sheaths)**.
- **Tendon healing:** inflammatory (days), proliferative (**type III collagen**, weeks), remodelling (**type III replaced by type I**, months); **never reaches original strength (about 70-80%)**.
- **Tendinopathy:** **failed healing response** (**not inflammation: "tendinosis"**): **disorganised collagen, increased ground substance, neovascularisation with nerve ingrowth (pain)**. **Continuum model (Cook and Purdam): reactive tendinopathy, tendon disrepair, degenerative tendinopathy**.
- **Treatment:** **load management, eccentric (Alfredson) or heavy slow resistance programmes (best evidence)**; **isometrics for pain relief**; **ESWT**; **PRP** (inconsistent); **steroid injections around load-bearing tendons (Achilles, patellar): risk of rupture: avoid intratendinous**.
- **Fluoroquinolones** (ciprofloxacin): **tendinopathy/rupture (Achilles)**, especially **older patients, with corticosteroids, renal impairment**. **Statins** (possible).

## 3. Bone stress injuries
- **Stress fractures** (**fatigue fractures in normal bone** from repetitive loading) vs **insufficiency fractures** (normal load on abnormal bone).
- **Risk factors:** **sudden increase in training**, **female athlete triad/RED-S**, **low vitamin D**, **low BMI**, **military recruits**, **cavus feet**, leg-length discrepancy, hard surfaces, poor footwear.
- **Imaging:** radiographs often normal initially (**periosteal reaction after 2-3 weeks**); **MRI (most sensitive and specific; Fredericson grading 1-4)**; bone scan (sensitive, non-specific).
- **High-risk stress fractures (tension side, poor blood supply: prone to non-union/displacement: often surgery or strict non-weight-bearing):**
  - **Femoral neck (tension: superolateral)**,
  - **Anterior cortex of the mid-tibia ("dreaded black line")** (**jumpers**; IM nailing if not healing),
  - **Medial malleolus**,
  - **Talus (lateral process)**,
  - **Navicular (central third: avascular)**: **CT**; **non-weight-bearing cast 6-8 weeks** or **screw fixation** in athletes,
  - **Proximal fifth metatarsal (Jones/zone 2-3: metaphyseal-diaphyseal junction)**: **intramedullary screw** in athletes,
  - **Sesamoids of the hallux**,
  - **Patella**,
  - **Base of the second metatarsal (ballet dancers)**.
- **Low-risk (compression side):** **posteromedial tibia (commonest stress fracture overall)**, **metatarsal shafts (2nd and 3rd: "march fracture")**, femoral shaft, **fibula**, calcaneus, **femoral neck compression side (inferomedial)**: **relative rest, modified activity**.
- **Medial tibial stress syndrome ("shin splints")**: **diffuse posteromedial tibial pain (distal two-thirds)**, **periostitis/traction of the soleus/FDL/tibialis posterior**; **MRI: periosteal oedema without fracture line**; rest, gradual return, **correct training errors**.
- **Chronic exertional compartment syndrome (CECS):** **anterior compartment commonest (then deep posterior)**; **pain with exercise, relieved by rest, ± numbness/foot drop**; **compartment pressure testing**: **(Pedowitz criteria) pre-exercise ≥15 mmHg, 1 minute post-exercise ≥30 mmHg, or 5 minutes post-exercise ≥20 mmHg**; **fasciotomy** (anterior and lateral; **superficial peroneal nerve** at risk where it pierces the fascia about **10-12 cm above the lateral malleolus**).
- **Popliteal artery entrapment syndrome** (young athletes: claudication; **medial head of gastrocnemius anomaly**), **external iliac artery endofibrosis** (cyclists): differentials of exertional leg pain.

## 4. Female athlete triad / RED-S
- **Female athlete triad (ACSM): low energy availability (with or without disordered eating), menstrual dysfunction (functional hypothalamic amenorrhoea), low bone mineral density** (**each on a spectrum**).
- **Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (RED-S, IOC 2014; updated 2023)**: broader concept affecting **both sexes**, multiple systems (**metabolic, haematological, cardiovascular, psychological, immunological, growth and development, performance**).
- **Low energy availability: under about 30 kcal/kg fat-free mass/day.**
- **Bone:** **low BMD (Z-score under -1.0 in athletes is concerning; under -2.0 = low BMD for age)** (use **Z-scores**, not T-scores, in premenopausal women and young athletes), **stress fractures (trabecular sites: femoral neck, sacrum, pelvis)**.
- **Treatment:** **multidisciplinary** (sports physician, dietitian, psychologist); **increase energy intake/reduce training**: restoration of menses; **oral contraceptive pills do not restore BMD** (mask amenorrhoea); **transdermal oestrogen** may be used if needed; calcium and vitamin D.

## 5. Concussion (sport-related)
- **Traumatic brain injury induced by biomechanical forces**: **functional rather than structural** (normal standard neuroimaging); symptoms may evolve over hours.
- **Signs:** loss of consciousness (**under 10%**), **amnesia**, confusion, headache, dizziness, balance problems, visual disturbance, **"just not right"**.
- **Assessment:** **SCAT6 (Sport Concussion Assessment Tool; Amsterdam 2022 consensus)** for athletes 13 years and older; **Child SCAT6** for 8-12 years; **Concussion Recognition Tool (CRT6)** for non-medical people.
- **"If in doubt, sit them out": no return to play on the same day.**
- **Red flags (immediate removal and emergency referral):** neck pain/tenderness, **double vision**, weakness/tingling in limbs, **severe or increasing headache**, **seizure**, **loss of consciousness**, **deteriorating conscious state**, **vomiting**, increasingly restless/agitated/combative.
- **Return to sport (graduated, stepwise):** **relative rest for 24-48 hours** (light activity encouraged), then **symptom-limited activity, aerobic exercise, sport-specific exercise, non-contact training drills, full-contact practice (after medical clearance), return to sport**; **at least 24 hours per step**; **children/adolescents: more conservative; return to learn before return to sport**.
- **Second impact syndrome:** **diffuse cerebral swelling** after a second concussion before recovery from the first: **adolescents**; often fatal.
- **Chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE):** tauopathy associated with repetitive head impacts (contact sports).

## 6. Pre-participation evaluation and cardiac issues
- **Sudden cardiac death in young athletes:** **hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (commonest in US athletes)**, **arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (Italy)**, **coronary artery anomalies**, **myocarditis**, **Marfan syndrome (aortic dissection)**, **commotio cordis** (blunt chest impact during repolarisation: **ventricular fibrillation**; **immediate CPR + AED**), **long QT**, **Brugada**, **WPW**.
- **Screening:** history and examination (AHA 14-point) ± **ECG (European/IOC practice)**.
- **Athlete's heart (physiological)**: sinus bradycardia, **first-degree AV block**, early repolarisation, isolated voltage criteria for LVH: **normal ECG variants in athletes (international criteria)**.
- **Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction**, **exertional heat stroke** (**core temperature over 40 C + CNS dysfunction**: **cold-water immersion ("cool first, transport second")**), **hyponatraemia (exercise-associated: over-drinking hypotonic fluids in endurance events)**.
- **Marfan:** avoid contact and isometric sports (aortic root dilatation).
- **Atlantoaxial instability in Down syndrome** (screening for contact sports, Special Olympics).
- **Return to play after infectious mononucleosis:** **splenic rupture risk (days 4-21)**: **avoid contact sports for at least 3-4 weeks** (until splenomegaly resolves).

## 7. Anti-doping
### Organisation
- **World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA)**: founded **1999** (after the 1998 Tour de France Festina scandal); publishes the **World Anti-Doping Code** and the **Prohibited List** (updated **annually, effective 1 January**).
- **National anti-doping organisations:** **India: NADA (National Anti-Doping Agency, established 2005)**; **National Dope Testing Laboratory (NDTL), New Delhi**; **National Anti-Doping Act, 2022**.
- **Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS)**: appeals.
### Criteria for inclusion on the Prohibited List (any two of three)
1. **Potential to enhance sport performance.**
2. **Actual or potential health risk to the athlete.**
3. **Violates the spirit of sport.**
- (Or masks the use of other prohibited substances.)
### Prohibited List categories
- **Prohibited at all times (in and out of competition):**
  - **S0 Non-approved substances**,
  - **S1 Anabolic agents** (**anabolic androgenic steroids**: testosterone, **nandrolone**, **stanozolol**; **other anabolic agents: clenbuterol, SARMs, tibolone, zeranol**),
  - **S2 Peptide hormones, growth factors and related substances** (**EPO and erythropoiesis-stimulating agents**, **HIF activators** (e.g. **roxadustat**, **cobalt**), **hCG and LH (in males)**, **growth hormone and its releasing factors**, **IGF-1**, corticotrophins),
  - **S3 Beta-2 agonists** (all prohibited, **except inhaled salbutamol (max 1,600 µg/24 h, not exceeding 600 µg over 8 hours)**, **inhaled formoterol (max 54 µg/24 h)**, **inhaled salmeterol (max 200 µg/24 h)**, **inhaled vilanterol (max 25 µg/24 h)** within therapeutic doses),
  - **S4 Hormone and metabolic modulators** (**aromatase inhibitors** (anastrozole, letrozole), **SERMs** (tamoxifen, clomiphene), **myostatin inhibitors**, **insulin and insulin mimetics**, **meldonium**, **trimetazidine**, **AICAR, GW1516 (PPAR-delta agonists)**),
  - **S5 Diuretics and masking agents** (**furosemide, thiazides, spironolactone, acetazolamide**, **desmopressin**, **probenecid**, **plasma expanders: albumin, dextran, HES**, **mannitol IV**) (**drospirenone, pamabrom, topical dorzolamide/brinzolamide are permitted**),
  - **M1 Manipulation of blood and blood components** (**blood doping: autologous, allogenic, homologous transfusion**; artificial oxygen carriers),
  - **M2 Chemical and physical manipulation** (**tampering, urine substitution**, **IV infusions/injections over 100 mL per 12-hour period** except during hospital treatment, surgery or clinical investigations),
  - **M3 Gene and cell doping**.
- **Prohibited in competition only:**
  - **S6 Stimulants** (amphetamines, cocaine, **ephedrine (over 10 µg/mL urine)**, **pseudoephedrine (over 150 µg/mL)**, methylhexaneamine, modafinil, **methylphenidate**, strychnine) (**caffeine, nicotine, phenylephrine, synephrine are on the monitoring programme, not prohibited**),
  - **S7 Narcotics** (morphine, oxycodone, fentanyl, methadone, pethidine, **tramadol (prohibited in competition since 2024)**) (**codeine permitted**),
  - **S8 Cannabinoids** (**except cannabidiol (CBD)**; THC urinary threshold **150 ng/mL**),
  - **S9 Glucocorticoids** (**all injectable routes, oral, rectal** prohibited in competition; **inhaled, topical, intranasal are permitted**; **washout periods** for injections, e.g. about 3 days intramuscular/intra-articular for most).
- **Prohibited in particular sports:** **P1 Beta-blockers** (**archery, shooting (also out of competition)**, golf, billiards, darts, motorsport, skiing (some disciplines), underwater sports).
- **Local anaesthetics (lidocaine), NSAIDs, paracetamol, insulin for diabetes (with TUE), vitamins** are not prohibited (insulin requires TUE).

### Anti-doping rule violations (ADRVs: 11 under the Code)
- **Presence of a prohibited substance** in a sample (**strict liability: the athlete is responsible for any substance found, regardless of intent**), use/attempted use, **evading/refusing sample collection**, **whereabouts failures (3 within 12 months)**, tampering, possession, trafficking, administration, complicity, prohibited association, **intimidating/retaliating against whistle-blowers**.
- **Sanctions:** **standard 4 years** for intentional violations involving non-specified substances; **2 years** if not intentional; **reduced for "no significant fault"** or **contaminated products**; **lifetime ban** for repeat serious violations.
- **Athlete Biological Passport (ABP):** **longitudinal monitoring of biomarkers** (haematological module: haemoglobin, reticulocytes, **OFF-score**; steroidal module: **testosterone/epitestosterone (T/E) ratio (over 4 suspicious)**; endocrine module (GH)); detects doping indirectly.
- **Testing methods:** urine and blood; **isotope ratio mass spectrometry (IRMS: exogenous testosterone)**, **GC-MS/LC-MS**, **dried blood spots**.

### Therapeutic Use Exemption (TUE)
- **Criteria (all must be met):**
  1. **Significant health impairment** without the substance,
  2. **No more than return to normal health** (no additional performance enhancement),
  3. **No reasonable permitted therapeutic alternative**,
  4. Not a consequence of prior non-therapeutic use of a prohibited substance.
- **Apply in advance** (retroactive TUE for emergencies). Examples: **insulin (diabetes)**, **glucocorticoids (systemic)**, **methylphenidate (ADHD)**, **testosterone (genuine hypogonadism)**, **beta-blockers in shooting (cardiac indication)**.

### Doctor's responsibilities
- **Check every medication against the current Prohibited List** (e.g. **Global DRO**, NADA app), **record medications**, **advise on supplements (contamination risk: anabolic agents/stimulants in supplements)**, **apply for TUE**, **IV infusion limits**; **doctors can be sanctioned** (administration, complicity).

## 8. Other sports medicine topics
- **Platelet-rich plasma (PRP)**: autologous platelet concentrate (**growth factors: PDGF, TGF-beta, VEGF**); **not prohibited by WADA** (growth factors within PRP: **permitted since 2011**); evidence best for **knee OA and lateral epicondylitis** (mixed).
- **Exercise prescription:** **WHO 2020: adults 150-300 minutes moderate or 75-150 minutes vigorous aerobic activity per week + muscle-strengthening 2 or more days/week**.
- **Athletes and NSAIDs:** may impair **bone and tendon-bone healing** (fracture non-union concern), **renal injury with dehydration**.
- **Sports drinks and carbohydrate loading**; **creatine** (not prohibited; increases phosphocreatine stores: short-burst power).

> Exam pearl: **WADA (1999) Prohibited List annual (1 January); India: NADA (2005), NDTL, National Anti-Doping Act 2022. Inclusion = any 2 of 3: performance, health risk, spirit of sport. Strict liability. Standard intentional sanction 4 years. Whereabouts: 3 failures in 12 months.**

> Exam pearl: **At all times: anabolic agents, EPO/HIF activators, GH, beta-2 agonists (except inhaled salbutamol under 1,600 µg/day, formoterol, salmeterol), aromatase inhibitors/SERMs, insulin, meldonium, diuretics/masking agents, blood doping, IV infusion over 100 mL/12 h, gene doping. In competition: stimulants, narcotics (tramadol since 2024; codeine allowed), cannabinoids (CBD allowed), systemic/injected glucocorticoids. Beta-blockers in archery/shooting. TUE: health impairment, no enhancement, no alternative.**

> Exam pearl: **High-risk stress fractures: femoral neck tension side, anterior tibia (dreaded black line), navicular, Jones (5th MT proximal), medial malleolus, sesamoids. RED-S: use Z-scores; OCP does not restore BMD. Concussion: no same-day return, SCAT6, stepwise return at least 24 h per step. Commotio cordis: AED.**
